title: The golden mouth
hookLine: John Chrysostom: if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice

lines: A HUNGRY MAN AT THE DOOR.
cards: Silk in the church. Gold cups for the wine. A preacher stands in a church full of beautiful things, and he points past all of it, to the door, and to the man sitting outside it, asking for bread.
The preacher is John, a priest of Antioch who later became bishop of Constantinople. People came to call him Chrysostom, which means golden mouth.

teach.b: The sermon is one of his homilies on Matthew's Gospel. He's speaking of the bread and the cup, the body of Christ at the altar, with deep reverence. Then he turns.
Do you want to honor Christ's body? Then don't ignore him when he's naked. Don't honor him in here with silk, while outside you pass him by, cold and without clothes.
What good is it if his table is loaded with gold cups, while he himself is dying of hunger? Feed him first. Then adorn his table too.
He isn't against beautiful churches. He's against the order being backwards. Where does he get this?

At the end of a story about the last judgment, the King says, in the King James words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Chrysostom takes that at its word.

teach.h: THE SAME CHRIST, AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: The person at the door isn't only a reminder of Christ; by that Gospel, what's done to him is done to Christ. The same Christ the congregation is about to receive at the altar is sitting outside, asking.
Churches understand the altar differently. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways.

All of them can hear Chrysostom's question about the door. The golden mouth didn't keep him safe. His preaching against luxury, the luxury of the powerful included, made him enemies, and he died in exile.
His sermons are still read, and the question is still in them: did you see him at the door?

how: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy that bears John Chrysostom's name, and Christians of different churches honor him as a saint and read his sermons, especially on care for the poor.

o: a bishop's silk robe, worn on great feast days
golden mouth, a name given to the preacher John
a gold cup used for the wine at the altar

games.q: what's inside the sermon — tap the pairs.
p: while Christ is dying of hunger
ye have done it unto me

s: it's a nickname people gave him. it means golden mouth.
Chrysostom told people to strip their churches bare
he said feed Christ first when he's hungry, then adorn his table.
his preaching against luxury made him enemies, and he died far from his church.

games.q: you have money to give. the altar needs new gold cups, and a man outside the church is hungry. what does Chrysostom say?
o: the cups first: honor God's house.
feed him first, then adorn the table.
games.why: feed Christ when he's hungry, he says, then adorn his table. he isn't against beauty; he's against the order being backwards.

practice: Recall someone you've passed who was asking, on a corner, at a station, outside a shop; maybe you gave, maybe you looked away, and there's no verdict either way.
See their face again, as a face, and settle on one concrete thing for next time: a coin, a sandwich, a question about their name. If you pray, pray for that person, even without a name.

wordCard.voice: Chrysostom, the golden mouth. John, the preacher who said the Christ honored at the altar is also asking at the door.

orig.note: Greek: golden-mouthed. the name people gave John the preacher.

carryVoice: Your line: christ at the door. The same Christ, at the altar and outside it. That's day seven hundred eighty-two.
